structure.title: Dedication – Prologue in Heaven · Three thresholds before Faust's room
structure.text: A dedication looks back to lost companions. A theatre director argues with a poet and a comic actor. A heavenly prologue turns a man's future into the subject of a wager. Faust first appears after other people have had ample time to frame his story.

structure.title: Night – Witch’s Kitchen · From study to street
structure.text: Learned beyond almost everyone he knows, Faust still experiences his knowledge as deprivation. Mephistopheles offers company and a way out. Their bargain turns on the precise circumstances under which Faust might ever want an instant to last.

structure.title: Street – Dungeon · Gretchen's town
structure.text: In courtyards, gardens and a church, Faust's appetite for experience meets a young woman with a family, a faith and a reputation to lose. His infernal companion can arrange a meeting. The burden of what happens afterwards falls very unevenly.

people.name: Faust and Mephistopheles
people.text: Faust wants to experience everything a human being can. Mephistopheles has a gift for supplying a decidedly small or vulgar answer to a magnificent demand. Their banter can disguise the amount of work being done on other people.

people.name: Margarete (Gretchen)
people.role: A young woman Faust meets in the street
people.text: Her daily round includes housework, family obligations and church. She asks Faust a remarkably direct question about religion, on a subject where the celebrated scholar finds a straight answer difficult.

prerequisites.title: The Book of Job, chapters 1–2
prerequisites.text: Goethe's Prologue in Heaven is modelled on the opening of Job, where the Lord allows a tempter to test a faithful man. These two short chapters show what kind of wager is being made over Faust, and how Goethe changes its terms.

context.title: Two wagers with different stakes
context.text: In the heavenly prologue, Mephistopheles expects to lead a striving man astray. Later Faust sets terms of his own. He has heard nothing of the first exchange, an advantage in knowledge that the audience shares with his companion.

notice.text: Where do the gifts come from?
notice.why: Jewellery can enter a private room without its owner seeing the transaction. Admiration in front of a mirror exists alongside a poverty that makes the gift both exciting and hard to refuse.

notice.text: Listen to Gretchen singing while she works.
notice.why: A repeated line can register longing in the rhythm of a tool or an ordinary task. Her experience of time has little in common with Faust's freedom to move on to the next scene.

opening: Faust has studied everything he thought would make life worth living and finds himself trapped in a room full of books. He wants experience powerful enough to break through his disgust. Mephistopheles offers assistance, with terms attached, and the scholar's hunger acquires opportunities it has never had before. Goethe turns intellectual disappointment into a dangerous appetite for the world, where another person's innocence can become part of a man's experiment in finally feeling alive. The devil is excellent company while the costs accumulate.
